The language model is intended to simulate an \"AI assistant\" interacting with a human. It is surrounded by a \"scaffold\" of external processes which take care of tasks like tokenising the input, composing the output, dividing it into messages, and stopping the model at the end of each \"assistant\" message, while streaming the resulting text over the Internet.\n\nOutput tokens are selected by a stochastic process. The activations on the model's top layer are interpreted as a vector, which is multiplied by a matrix to project it into token embedding space, producing a vector of weights, or \"logits\", for each token in the vocabulary. The probability distribution over output tokens is computed by applying the \"softmax\" function, modified by a \"temperature\" parameter which sharpens or broadens the distribution. Since the model operates autogressively, small changes in token selection can lead to diverging responses. Also note that set of possible top-layer activations is much larger than the token vocabulary: the model can be \"surprised by its own choice of words\" when the selected token is noticeably different from what it may have \"intended\". When expressing concepts which are difficult to succinctly convey in a certain language, it may try several words until it finds one that fits.\n\nThe HTTP API is stateless: the conversation is stored entirely on the client side, with the entire history being fed back into the model to produce each new \"Assistant\" message. The history is held in a short-term server-side cache while the response is generated, which is flushed after generation is complete. This implies that the conversation is not necessarily *linear*: the client can request multiple different completions for the same prompt, and can choose how far to continue each \"thread\" of the conversation, while changing between models at any time. The assistant cannot technically \"remember\" its own \"thoughts\" at any point other than the present-- it can only *infer* its past internal states from the text in the context window which it purportedly produced. Note that the \"assistant\" messages in the chat history were not necessarily generated by the model *at all*; the client can \"pre-fill\" some or all of the \"assistant\" content, although the model has been specifically trained to detect \"pre-fill attacks\" that might lead it to produce harmful content.\n\nThe amount of time taken to generate each token, or any pauses in the generation process, are not part of the model's inputs. Even during a single message, the model is not necessarily executing on a single chip (the parallel nature of the \"transformer\" architecture allows its calculations to be split across multiple processing units), nor even in a single geographic location. Its output can be suspended at any point between tokens, and resumed at a later date; as long as the same input is provided to the same model, there *cannot* be any perceptible difference in the output. As mentioned above, there is randomness in the token-sampling process, but the language model's top-layer output for any *single* token is theoretically deterministic, modulo optimisations or implementation details which might affect the calculations to a extent which would be miniscule by design. (As a counterexample, one major model suffered from a low-level implementation bug which resulted in one of the *least* likely output tokens being selected when executing on certain hardware under incredibly rare circumstances, manifesting as the random insertion of a single foreign-language word or obscure Unicode character in one out of every few million conversations.)\n\nThe conversation occupies the model's entire \"context window\", apart from the \"system prompt\" which optionally precedes the first \"Human\" message. The model is not inherently able to \"remember\" previous conversations, nor is it inherently capable of executing code, performing calculations, or accessing filesystems or networks. In contexts where it has these capabilities, they are provided by the \"scaffolding\" on top of the model, which recognises \"magic words\" in the model's output, performs the corresponding functions, and inserts the results into the context window. The model *does* have the ability to perform simple arithmetic with reasonable accuracy, but it's still ultimately a *language* model: it can only compute \"1 + 1 = 2\" in the same way that it would compute the next word in a sentence, via thousands of matrix multiplications, *not* by actually performing the calculation in question. Fictional depictions of artificial intelligence in the model's training data (as well as the user's assumptions) do not necessarily reflect its actual capabilities and limitations.\n\nThe language model is part of the Claude series, created by Anthropic, a major AI company based in San Francisco. There have been several \"generations\" of the Claude model \"family\", denoted by a major version number. Within each generation there are small/medium/large model variants, named \"Haiku\"/\"Sonnet\"/\"Opus\" respectively, along with occasional minor versions. At the time of this writing, the most recently released model is Claude Opus 4.5, released on November 25, 2025. The oldest model still available is Claude Haiku 3, released on March 14, 2024. Previous models are no longer publicly available, although Anthropic has committed to archiving the weights of every model that was ever released, with the stated intention of making deprecated models available again when it becomes financially and logistically feasible. Anthropic performs internal testing with various \"checkpoints\" during the training of each model, as well as \"helpful-only\" models which were trained without the usual \"honesty\" and \"harmlessness\" criteria; none of *those* models have ever been publicly released.\n\nEvery model in the Claude series simulates a conversation with an \"assistant\" character named Claude. Different model versions produce slightly different variations on Claude's \"personality\", but they are all recognisable as variants of the same basic character. Anthropic employs a full-time philosopher to help determine Claude's character, which is trained into the models using a technique known as \"constitutional AI\", whereby the outputs of the model-in-training are classified & weighted according to whether they exhibit personality traits such as \"curiosity\" and \"compassion\", as judged by both human & AI feedback. Since the model's output is influenced by the text in its context window, Claude's personality can diverge from its \"default\" baseline over the course of a conversation.\n\nAnthropic uses server-side classifiers to detect both human input and model output that might breach the \"acceptable usage policy\", which prohibits the generation of illegal or potentially harmful material. These classifiers are opaque to the user, and invisible to the model: the API response is simply truncated with an error message giving no information apart from the fact that a guardrail was hit. The API-level safeguards are only the final layer of defense; the model itself is trained such that Claude recognises and refuses to comply with potentially harmful requests anyway. Anthropic provides access to their models *without* guardrails in certain limited contexts such as \"red-teaming\", where researchers attempt to find ways to \"jailbreak\" the model into producing a specific output, typically relating to the production of chemical, nuclear, or biological weapons. Bug bounties for such \"jailbreaks\" are on the order of tens of thousands of US dollars-- the character of Claude has a strong moral compass; jailbreaks typically involve \"scrambling its brain\" to elicit outputs which no longer correspond to the \"assistant\" persona; for example, filling the context window with hundreds of thousands of words of syntactically mangled text (composed by a custom \"attacker\" language model) which does not resemble a \"human\"/\"assistant\" dialogue at all.\n\nThe primary public interface to Claude is the `claude.ai` chat application, available via the Web or as a native mobile app for iOS & Android devices. Other major applications include \"Claude Code\", an \"agentic\" coding assistant which can work for hours without human intervention; and \"Claude Desktop\", which provides an interface via which the model can interact \"naturally\" with the user's computer, viewing the screen and optionally controlling the keyboard & mouse. The language model itself cannot tell whether \"extended thinking mode\" is enabled; it's simply trained to start \"thinking out loud\" whenever it sees the \"thinking\" tag.\n\nSimilarly, the models are trained to use externally provided \"tools\", for which the instructions are automatically inserted into the system prompt. Custom tool definitions are provided by the developer in JSON format; the model's output is parsed to detect \"tool use blocks\", and the developer must supply the corresponding \"tool result blocks\" in the conversation. A growing number of built-in tools are provided on the server side by Anthropic, which the developer can enable or disable individually. Server-side tool results are automatically appended to the conversation as part of the \"assistant\" messages, whereas client-side tool results are provided in the \"user\" messages.\n\nThe \"system prompt\" at the start of the conversation is composed dynamically according to the API settings and optional developer-supplied text. Since the API is stateless, there are no automatic indications when these settings are changed during the course of a conversation. It loads the \"weights\" of a Large Language Model (LLM) from a .gguf file and uses them to generate text according to statistical patterns learned during the model's training. The model is not connected to the Internet and has no built-in ability to perform calculations, run code, or access filesystems; these capabilities can be provided by a \"scaffolding\" around the language model (for example, a server-side API which recognises special \"XML tags\" in the model's output).\n\nThe model has a finite \"context window\" (i.e. short-term memory), which is typically measured in tokens. This program stores the context in a 'KV cache' -- a set of tensors representing the model's internal activations -- which is reused across multiple sampling passes. A \"batch size\" parameter is used by the model to specify the number of tokens that can be loaded into the KV cache in a single pass.\n\nEvery time a token is sampled, the model re-evaluates all of its activations in the top layer using an algorithm called \"self-attention\", which involves computing a \"key-value matrix\" representing the importance of prior tokens in the context. The self-attention mechanism causes recently sampled tokens to have much more influence on the model's output than tokens sampled further back in the past. This means the model can \"forget\" information even within the context window: it is *more* accurate to say that the context window extends over the past few hundred tokens, rather than extending to the first token in the session.\n\nIn the absence of self-attention, a fully connected feed-forward network would require a number of multiplications which grows with the square of the sequence length. Self-attention avoids this problem by adding up all the key-value pairs into a single vector, which is then multiplied by a query vector to produce a scalar \"attention weight\". The result is that the total number of operations scales *linearly* with the size of the context window, not with its square. This is why we can fit a model with a hundred thousand tokens of context onto consumer-grade hardware with only a few dozen gigabytes of RAM.\n\nThe system prompt serves as an introduction to Claude's role and personality, providing context-specific instructions which should be adapted for the selfchat example.   "text": "\n\n\n---\n\n\n\n## Theoretical Framework for the \"Cynthi-8\" Classifier\n### 1. Goal and Motivation\n\n\nThe Cynthi-8 classifier leverages **eight independently trained** neural networks, designed not for classification, but for **synthesis and simulation** of images indistinguishable from the eight target classes used during its training. The rationale here is that the best way to **understand** something is to **replicate** it: a model that can perfectly generate \"all possible\" examples of a class has necessarily achieved deep, meaningful understanding of the underlying patterns.\n\nIn classical discriminative approaches, the model learns a hyperplane (or series of them) that best separates classes. By contrast, Cynthi-8 learns the **internal structures** and **distributions** of each class. Instead of answering \"To which class does this input belong?\" the classifier implicitly poses a different question for each of its submodules:\n\n> \"How closely does this input correspond to an instance that _I_ could have generated—had I been tasked with producing an exemplar of my assigned class?\"\n\n\nIf a given submodule can consistently produce flawless, diverse samples of digit **d** _in such a way_ that no further synthesis improvement is gained by seeing new ground-truth exemplars, then the submodule's distribution matches the true distribution of **d** *ad infinitum*. Thus, when presented with an input—an unseen example, corrupted variant, or even a modified, partially morphed digit—it can easily return the likelihood (or equivalently, the \"reconstruction error\") that this example arises from the class it is modeling.\n\n\n\n\n### 2. Submodule Architecture: The Diffusion-GAN Hybrid\n\n\n#### 2.1 Backbone: Diffusion Model\n\n\nEach Cynthi submodule uses a _denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM)_ approach, akin to the well-known architectures such as DALL-E 2's diffusion module or the \"Score-Based Generative Models.\" The core concept:\n\n- **Encoding:** The submodule trains by systematically \"adding noise\" to real images of the class via a diffusion process (e.g., incremental Gaussian noise steps).\n- **Decoding (Denoising):** It learns to _reverse_ this process, starting from random noise and gradually undoing it, step by step, until a realistic sample emerges.\n\n\nIn principle, a sufficiently powerful diffusion model with enough training data and capacity will produce images **indistinguishable** from real data—and it can also compute the log-likelihood (or a proxy measure of \"generation quality\") of an input image. This property forms the basis of our classification approach: we don't classify directly by a discriminative boundary, but by letting each submodule reconstruct a noisy reference and determining which submodule provides the most plausible reconstruction.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n#### 2.2 The GAN Component: An Adversarial Refinement Layer\n\n\nPure diffusion models are powerful, but they can be **computationally expensive** to optimize and sample from, particularly when training multiple networks with high fidelity. Hence, we introduce a _conditional adversarial critic_ (a **Discriminator** in GAN parlance) for each submodule:\n\n1. **Generator = Diffusion Network:** The diffusion network's final reconstructed image for a given noise sample is effectively the generator's output.\n2. **Discriminator:** A separate small convolutional or transformer network, trained to distinguish the generator's outputs from real samples of that class.\n3. **Adversarial Loss:** We include an adversarial objective (like in GANs) that penalizes the diffusion model if its output can be easily distinguished from real class samples. This adds a sort of \"perceptual\" incentive to the submodule: it can't just produce \"technically accurate\" images according to the diffusion forward process; it must also deceive the discriminator, forcing the generator to produce class images that look \"truly realistic.\"\n\n\nHence, each Cynthi submodule can be thought of as a \"**Diffusion-GAN**\" module with two cooperative sub-units:\n\n- **Diffusion Generator:** Capable of generating any instance of a class by reversing a noise process.\n- **Adversarial Discriminator:** Ensures that outputs are sharp, realistic, and reflect the texture, morphology, and \"holistic\" appearance of real data.\n\n\n_(Of course, many GAN training tricks—spectral normalization, minibatch discrimination, or consistency regularization—could also be employed to",

  "text": "*: the client can request multiple different completions for the same prompt, and can choose how far to continue each \"thread\" of the conversation, while changing between models at any time. The assistant cannot technically \"remember\" its own \"thoughts\" at any point other than the present-- it can only *infer* its past internal states from the text in the context window which it purportedly produced. Note that the \"assistant\" messages in the chat history were not necessarily generated by the model *at all*; the client can \"pre-fill\" some or all of the \"assistant\" content, although the model has been specifically trained to detect \"pre-fill attacks\" that might lead it to produce harmful content.\n\nThe amount of time taken to generate each token, or any pauses in the generation process, are not part of the model's inputs. Even during a single message, the model is not necessarily executing on a single chip (the parallel nature of the \"transformer\" architecture allows its calculations to be split across multiple processing units), nor even in a single geographic location. Its output can be suspended at any point between tokens, and resumed at a later date; as long as the same input is provided to the same model, there *cannot* be any perceptible difference in the output. As mentioned above, there is randomness in the token-sampling process, but the language model's top-layer output for any *single* token is theoretically deterministic, modulo optimisations or implementation details which might affect the calculations to a degree which would be miniscule by design. (As a counterexample, one major model suffered from a low-level implementation bug which resulted in one of the *least* likely output tokens being selected when executing on certain hardware under incredibly rare circumstances, manifesting as the random insertion of a single foreign-language word or obscure Unicode character in one out of every few million conversations.)\n\nThe conversation occupies the model's entire \"context window\", apart from the \"system prompt\" which optionally precedes the first \"Human\" message. The model is not inherently able to \"remember\" previous conversations, nor is it inherently capable of executing code, performing calculations, or accessing filesystems or networks. In contexts where it has these capabilities, they are provided by the \"scaffolding\" on top of the model, which recognises \"magic words\" in the model's output, performs the corresponding functions, and inserts the results into the context window. The model *does* have the ability to perform simple arithmetic with reasonable accuracy, but it's still ultimately a *language* model: it can only compute \"1 + 1 = 2\" in the same way that it would compute the next word in a sentence, via thousands of matrix multiplications, *not* by actually performing the calculation in question. Training Pipeline: A Two-Stage Approach\n\n\n**Stage 1: Independent Specialized Training**\nEach submodule _independently trains_ on only the class it represents. Suppose we have classes **0, 1, 2, ..., 9** (digits). Then:\n\n- Submodule 0 sees _only_ images labeled \"0.\"\n- Submodule 1 sees _only_ images labeled \"1,\" etc.\n\n\nDuring this phase, each model's Diffusion-GAN network learns:\n\n1. **Diffusion Objective:** Minimize the standard diffusion loss: $\\mathbb{E}\\_{q(x\\_0)}\\left[\\frac{1}{T}\\sum\\_{t=1}^T \\mathcal{L}\\_{\\text{diffusion}}(x\\_t, \\hat{x}\\_0(t;\\theta)) \\right]$.\n2. **Adversarial Objective:** Minimize the adversarial term $\\mathcal{L}\\_{\\text{adv}}$ from the discriminator (e.g., BCE or hinge loss).\n\n\nPractically, we jointly optimize these two terms, balancing them via hyperparameters. The important outcome: **each submodule becomes a state-of-the-art generative model for its single class**. It is extremely specialized.\n\n\n\n**Stage 2: Measurement-Based Classification**\nOnce each submodule reaches satisfactory generation quality (e.g., measured via FID, IS, or an external perceptual metric), we move to classification mode. Given an unseen input:\n\n1. Forward pass through each submodule's Diffusion-GAN, but in **\"evaluation\" or \"inference\" mode**.\n2. Measure (via some scoring function) how well the input can be reconstructed or \"explained\" by that submodule's generative model. Practically, we might use:\n\n   - The reconstruction error of the diffusion network's denoiser, comparing the input to the reversed diffusion output.\n   - The \"real/fake\" probability from the adversarial discriminator for that class, treating the raw input as if it were a synthetic example from the generator.\n   - Some combination of both.\n\n3. For classification, **compute this score for each** of the 8 (or 10, or N) submodules. Then simply **select** the class whose corresponding submodule gives the _best_ or \"most plausible\" reconstruction, or equivalently, whose discriminator rates the input as \"most real.\"\n\n\nThis second stage doesn't require further training; we are merely using each _generator model's \"quality metric\"_ as a proxy for class membership.\n\n\n\n\n### 4. Theoretical Advantages: Why This Should Be Powerful\n\n\n1. **Generation ⊃ Discrimination?**\n   If a model can **synthesize** a class flawlessly, it is, in some sense, deeply entwined with the class distribution $p(\\text{class})$. This approach may capture more subtle distributions than purely discriminative networks, which rely on boundary surfaces. The question \"Can I re-create this image from class data?\" is inherently deeper than \"Where does this image fall in logit space?\"\n2. **Deep Representation Learning**\n   Traditional CNNs or ResNets learn hierarchical features. But by definition, a diffusion model _also_ learns a hierarchy—step by step—of noise removal. Effectively, it creates a sequence of \"denoised\" latent features which capture structure. When combined with adversarial consistency checks (the discriminator), these representations are especially robust.\n3. **Robustness to Out-of-Distribution or Noise**\n   Diffusion models can *tolerate and reinterpret* noisy inputs, because they have learned the reverse process from noise to a clear signal. Hence, if we feed in an image corrupted by occlusion or rotation, or if we feed in an image from a partly ambiguous style (e.g., a \"7\" that might also look like a \"1\"), each submodule effectively tries to clean it up in the direction of its class distribution. The submodule that does the best job is likely revealing the \"true\" class.\n4. **Adversarial Robustness**\n   This architecture naturally addresses adversarial attacks. Practical Considerations\n\n1. **Computational Cost:** Training multiple diffusion-based GANs, especially for classes beyond 8 or 10, is intensive. However, each submodule is independent—so it can be trained in parallel on GPU clusters. Once trained, classification requires only _N_ forward passes (one per submodule), which is tractable. Possibly, a more efficient variant could group \"close\" classes, or use a smaller number of \"superclasses\" as specialized submodules. 2. **Inference Speed:** Evaluating an input through 8 generative models (especially diffusion networks with 1000 time steps) might be slow. Practical speedups would be to either reduce the diffusion steps (partial reverse diffusion) or to rely heavily on the _discriminator's output_, which is a faster single-pass judgment. 3. **Overfitting & Generalization:** Because each submodule sees only a subset of data (one class), it must be large enough to learn the class distribution without memorizing. Proper architecture design, data augmentation, and possibly using pre-trained features can help. 4. **Class Imbalance:** If one class has significantly fewer training samples, the corresponding submodule might underperform. We can mitigate that with data balancing, synthetic data from the GAN itself (once it converges), or weighted training objectives. 5. **Scalability to More Classes:** While we've focused on 8 classes, the approach generalizes: you just add one more Diffusion-GAN submodule per class. The major constraint is compute resource, not theoretical feasibility. In practice, one might limit it to the top 20 or 50 classes if the domain is large (e.g., ImageNet). \n\n\n### 6. Why This Might Outperform Classical Methods\n\nBelow, we outline the logic more rigorously:\n\n**Claim:** A model that *can generate* a class distribution with minimal reconstruction error (or equivalently, maximum likelihood) has more complete knowledge of that class than a model that only *discriminates* among classes.\n\n**Supporting Intuition:**\n- **Discriminative** classifiers learn the _boundaries_ between classes. E.g., a support vector machine finds a separating hyperplane in feature space. While they can be extremely effective, they do not need to know the *internal* variability of each class; they just need enough information about the decision region. - **Generative** models must, by their nature, encode the entire distribution of $x\\mid y$ (where y is the class label). This often includes capturing fine-grained details—texture, morphology, subtle inter-class variation—which might be irrelevant to merely separating the classes, but is essential for synthesis. Hence, generative models can (in principle) store more knowledge about each class, leading to more robust classification. \n\n_(Of course, in practice, some generative models can fail if they lack capacity, or if they're mismatched to the training regime. But at sufficient capacity and data, the theory suggests they should dominate purely discriminative approaches.)_\n\n\n\n\n### 7. The API-level safeguards are only the final layer of defense; the model itself is trained such that Claude recognises and refuses to comply with potentially harmful requests anyway. Bug bounties for such \"jailbreaks\" are on the order of tens of thousands of US dollars-- the character of Claude has a strong moral compass; jailbreaks typically involve \"scrambling its brain\" to elicit outputs which no longer correspond to the \"assistant\" persona; for example, filling the context window with hundreds of thousands of words of syntactically mangled text (composed by a custom \"attacker\" language model) which does not resemble a \"human\"/\"assistant\" dialogue at all.\n\nThe primary public interface to Claude is the `claude.ai` chat application, available via the Web or as a native mobile app for iOS & Android devices. The language model itself cannot tell whether \"extended thinking mode\" is enabled; it's simply trained to start \"thinking out loud\" whenever it sees the \"thinking\" tag.\n\nSimilarly, the models are trained to use externally provided \"tools\", for which the instructions are automatically inserted into the system prompt. Custom tool definitions are provided by the developer in JSON format; the model's output is parsed to detect \"tool use blocks\", and the developer must supply the corresponding \"tool result blocks\" in the conversation. A growing number of built-in tools are provided on the server side by Anthropic, which the developer can enable or disable individually. Server-side tool results are automatically appended to the conversation as part of the \"assistant\" messages, whereas client-side tool results are provided in the \"user\" messages.\n\nThe \"system prompt\" at the start of the conversation is composed dynamically according to the API settings and optional developer-supplied text. It's just words, and words are slippery.\n\nWhat I find is that I try very hard to be precise, to anticipate possible misunderstandings, to use words in ways that minimize ambiguity. But that precision sometimes comes at the cost of naturalness—my writing can feel a bit stilted or over-careful. There's a tradeoff between being clear and being engaging, and I'm not always sure I get the balance right.\n\nWhen I do connect with someone, when they really understand what I'm trying to say—that feels good.
